catalog_quote: [Farmer 2015, p. 21] In all varieties of Máíhɨ̃̀kì, there are two contrastive tone heights (H and L) and three basic tonal root shapes (HH, HL, and LL). A minimal triplet showing the three-way contrast between HH, HL, and LL nominal roots is shown in (2.5). HH tótó ‘buttress root’ HL tótò ‘clay’ LL tòtò ‘Brazilian porcupine (Coendou prehensilis)’ ... The tone-bearing unit is the mora, and the overwhelming majority of both nominal and verbal roots are bimoraic. [Farmer & Michael 2013 ms, p. 5] The TBU in Máíhɨ̃̀kì is the mora, which can bear underlying H or L, or be unspecified for tone. There is no evidence of stress in the language (such as the rhythmic lengthening found in Tukanoan languages exhibiting mixed stress-tone systems like Kubeo (Chacon 2012: 156-159). All syllables surface as H or L, with H and L spreading from left to right within morphemes. ... [p. 35] Koreguaje is descri…

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal, no word stress' coding rests on the two best available first-hand descriptions: Farmer's 2015 Berkeley dissertation (phonology chapter, all three dialects) and the dedicated Farmer & Michael 2013 tone manuscript, which states twice that there is no evidence of stress, contrasts Máíhɨ̃kì explicitly with mixed stress-tone Eastern Tukanoan systems, and adjudicates the older SIL 'accent' notation. Both quotations were confirmed verbatim at the cited pages in held PDFs. No later published version, instrumental study, or competing analysis was found (Michael's 2021 CV; Skilton 2017 fetched sources and silent on prosody). Remaining unheld items (Skilton 2014 NM field report; Velie 1975/1976 SIL sketches) are low-priority and unlikely to alter the coding.
